paragraphs: Training graph neural networks on large graphs can exceed GPU memory because the graph structure participates in the training computation. Many approaches try to make this manageable, but comparing them fairly is difficult. This paper organizes representative approaches into several families and builds a consistent benchmark to examine their tradeoffs.

The comparison combines mathematical analysis with measurements. The authors analyze the time and space requirements of the different families, then measure GPU memory consumption, processing throughput, and convergence. They also use a greedy search over hyperparameters to support consistent evaluation. Considering these aspects together helps explain whether a method's practical advantage comes from memory savings, faster processing, or its learning behavior.

The study then uses the strengths and weaknesses identified in this comparison to motivate EnGCN, an ensemble training approach. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on large-scale datasets. The contribution therefore includes both a framework for understanding existing scalable graph training methods and a new method informed by that comparison.
neurips-2022-a-comprehensive-study-on-la.tldr: A systematic benchmark of scalable graph training motivates EnGCN, an ensemble approach reported to achieve state-of-the-art performance on large-scale datasets.

paragraphs: Certified robustness training aims to produce classifiers with guarantees against adversarial attacks, but its computational cost makes it difficult to apply as datasets and networks grow. Repeated training adds another burden when new data arrive or architectures improve. This paper asks whether robustness already learned by one network can reduce the cost of training another.

The proposed framework, Certified Robustness Transfer, starts with a robust teacher model and trains a student using a loss designed to transfer the teacher's robustness. The central idea is to reuse this property through knowledge transfer. The authors present the framework as applicable across certified training methods and provide both theoretical and empirical support.

On CIFAR-10, the experiments report an average eightfold training speedup across three architecture generations while retaining robustness comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The authors also demonstrate scaling to ImageNet. These findings support robustness transfer as a way to make subsequent certified training less expensive, with an existing robust teacher serving as the starting resource.
neurips-2022-accelerating-certified-robu.tldr: Certified Robustness Transfer uses a robust teacher to accelerate student training, reporting an average eightfold speedup on CIFAR-10 with comparable robustness.

paragraphs: Blackbox adversarial attacks face a tradeoff: attacks transferred from other models need no victim feedback, while attacks guided by queries can succeed more often but require many interactions. BASES combines these approaches by using victim feedback to adjust how a fixed collection of surrogate models contributes to an attack.

Its perturbation generator minimizes a weighted loss across the surrogate models. The search then changes those weights using queries to the victim. This makes the number of search variables equal to the number of surrogate models, creating a small search space. The method concentrates scarce feedback on choosing an effective surrogate combination.

On the tested ImageNet classifiers, the authors report higher success rates with at least thirtyfold fewer queries than comparison methods. Reported results include over 90% targeted success with as few as three queries per image on average, and over 99% untargeted success with one to two queries. They also demonstrate attacks against Google Cloud Vision and object detectors, alongside transferability and applicability to hard-label attacks.
neurips-2022-blackbox-attacks-via-surrog.tldr: BASES searches over surrogate-model weights to produce successful blackbox adversarial attacks with very few victim-model queries in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A text generation API can be imitated by training another model on its outputs. Watermarks offer a way to check whether a suspected imitation inherited patterns from those outputs. This paper identifies a weakness in an earlier approach: statistical inspection of candidate words' frequencies can reveal the watermark.

CATER instead optimizes conditional word-selection rules. It seeks to keep the overall distribution of words largely unchanged while making their selection under particular conditions more distinctive. This separates the ownership signal from the simple frequency patterns that exposed earlier watermarks. The authors prove an infeasibility result for identifying the selected watermarks through statistical inspection of a large pool of potential word pairs, even with knowledge of the framework.

Empirically, higher-order conditions produce exponentially more suspicious but unused watermarks, helping conceal the actual choices. The authors also report effective infringement detection when imitation models use different architectures or domains, with negligible damage to output quality. The findings support conditional watermarking as a way to combine ownership verification with greater statistical concealment.
neurips-2022-cater-intellectual-property.tldr: CATER embeds ownership signals in conditional word choices while minimizing overall frequency changes, making its watermarks harder to uncover through statistical inspection.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether chaotic behavior during neural network training is merely undesirable instability or plays a useful role in optimization. It connects chaos to the curvature of the loss landscape and constructs a modified version of stochastic gradient descent that ensures non-chaotic training dynamics. That modification provides a way to study what changes when chaos is removed.

The empirical evidence suggests that eliminating the negative part of the curvature spectrum, associated with directions of local chaos, harms training performance. This supports a qualified conclusion: in the experiments, suppressing those dynamics carries a learning cost. The result makes the relationship between stable optimization and effective training more complicated than simply preferring less chaos.

The authors also examine longer-term behavior. Although most chaotic network behavior occurs early, models with slightly perturbed initializations continue to separate slowly after achieving top training performance. Their divergence can be modeled as a combination of random motion and linear separation. These observations challenge the picture of training trajectories eventually remaining within a confined parameter region.
neurips-2022-chaotic-dynamics-are-intrin.tldr: Experiments suggest that removing locally chaotic directions from SGD harms training, while initially perturbed models continue to diverge slowly after reaching top performance.

paragraphs: CLIPDraw turns a natural-language description into a drawing by using an existing language-image encoder to judge how closely the two match. The encoder is CLIP, and the method requires no additional training. The work explores how a pretrained model's assessment of text-image similarity can guide the creation of a new visual object.

The object being optimized is a collection of vector strokes. CLIP supplies a similarity measure between the rendered drawing and the description, and the synthesis process seeks to increase that similarity. The choice of strokes matters because it biases the result toward simpler shapes that people can recognize. The drawing representation therefore helps shape the output alongside the language-image model's guidance.

The paper compares CLIPDraw with other methods that generate images through optimization and examines interesting behaviors of its outputs. Its central contribution is this combination of a pretrained similarity measure and a stroke-based drawing representation. It illustrates a route from language to drawings in which generation happens through optimization without an additional training stage.
neurips-2022-clipdraw-exploring-text-to-.tldr: CLIPDraw creates vector-stroke drawings from text by optimizing their similarity under pretrained CLIP, without additional training.

paragraphs: Data augmentation can improve neural network learning, but applying expensive transformations across an entire dataset can be costly. This paper selects small subsets whose augmentation closely reproduces the training dynamics of augmenting all the data. The selection targets the effect that augmented examples have on learning.

The analysis models augmentation as additive perturbations. It shows how these perturbations strengthen and modify smaller singular values of the network Jacobian while preserving its prominent directions, helping with harder-to-learn information and overfitting. The method repeatedly selects subsets that preserve how the augmented Jacobian aligns with labels or prediction residuals. The authors prove similar SGD training dynamics for the selected augmented subsets and the fully augmented data.

Experiments report speedups of 6.3 times on CIFAR10 and 2.2 times on SVHN, with improvements over baselines of up to 10% across subset sizes. Results on TinyImageNet and ImageNet also show gains and speedups. On a label-corrupted CIFAR10 version, training with selected, augmented 50% subsets even outperforms using the full dataset.
neurips-2022-data-efficient-augmentation.tldr: Carefully selected training subsets can preserve the learning dynamics of full-data augmentation while substantially reducing computation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Source-free domain adaptation updates a pretrained model for a new domain without access to its original training data. Existing approaches either organize target examples into classes using predicted labels or emphasize consistency among nearby examples. The former can suffer from incorrect labels; the latter can retain biases from the source domain.

Divide and Contrast uses the source model's prediction confidence to split target examples into source-like and target-specific groups. The more reliable source-like examples support global class clustering. The noisier target-specific examples support learning local structure at the individual-example level. An adaptive contrastive learning framework gives these groups different learning goals according to their roles.

The method also uses a memory bank and a Maximum Mean Discrepancy loss to reduce the distribution mismatch between the groups. This connects their representations while preserving the distinction between their learning objectives. Experiments on VisDA, Office-Home, and DomainNet report better performance than existing state-of-the-art approaches, supporting the strategy of treating target examples differently according to confidence.
neurips-2022-divide-and-contrast-source-.tldr: Divide and Contrast adapts a model without source data by using confident target examples for class structure and noisier examples for local structure.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms learn which decisions work well from the feedback they receive. In censored environments, that feedback can be unavailable because people do not follow recommendations or information is lost or delayed. This paper studies how such censorship affects classical algorithms for both multi-armed and contextual bandits.

The authors introduce a broad family of censorship models and describe their statistical difficulty through an effective dimension. This quantity drives their bounds on regret, the performance lost through imperfect decisions during learning. Their formulation embeds the problem in a larger space while retaining its original structure at first order, allowing results analogous to those for uncensored feedback. The analysis uses a continuous generalization of the Elliptical Potential Inequality.

The results also distinguish two phases. An initial phase pays an extra cost while correcting misspecified censorship, followed by a stationary phase with a learning slowdown governed by effective dimension. This distinction helps separate the temporary cost of learning the feedback process from the continuing cost of receiving censored information.
neurips-2022-effective-dimension-in-band.tldr: The paper uses effective dimension to quantify how censored feedback slows bandit learning and separates initial correction costs from the continuing slowdown.

paragraphs: Machine learning systems sometimes need derivatives of an optimization problem's solution, as in optimization layers, hyperparameter tuning, and meta-learning. Computing these derivatives through implicit differentiation has often required mathematical derivations and specialized implementations for each problem. This paper proposes a reusable way to automate that work.

The user writes a Python function describing the problem's optimality conditions: the relationships that characterize a solution. The framework applies automatic differentiation to this function and uses the implicit function theorem to obtain derivatives of the optimization problem. This separates the specification of what makes a solution optimal from the machinery that computes its derivatives.

That separation also allows the differentiation mechanism to be added on top of an existing solver. The authors show how the framework recovers many established implicit differentiation methods and makes new ones easier to formulate. They demonstrate its use for bilevel optimization and sensitivity analysis in molecular dynamics. The practical contribution is a modular interface that brings solver-based computations into differentiable workflows.
neurips-2022-efficient-and-modular-impli.tldr: Automatic implicit differentiation computes derivatives of optimization solutions from user-written optimality conditions, separating differentiation from the choice of solver.

paragraphs: Federated learning allows several participants to train a model together while keeping their data in separate locations. In the cross-silo setting, there are relatively few reliable participants, each with a medium or large dataset. Healthcare is an important example, but the shortage of realistic benchmarks makes it harder to study algorithms for this setting.

FLamby addresses that gap with a suite of seven healthcare datasets. The datasets have natural splits and span different tasks, data types, and amounts of data. Each includes baseline training code. This gives researchers several settings in which to examine cross-silo learning, with partitions grounded in the datasets' existing organization.

The authors also benchmark standard federated learning algorithms across the full suite. Their contribution is a shared experimental resource and starting point for comparing methods. Its modular design supports downloading datasets, reproducing results, and reusing components in new research. Together, the datasets and code make it easier to investigate how federated approaches behave across varied healthcare problems.
neurips-2022-flamby-datasets-and-benchma.tldr: FLamby provides seven naturally partitioned healthcare datasets, training code, and benchmarks for studying cross-silo federated learning.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs describe how observed and hidden variables are generated. Posterior inference works in the opposite direction, estimating hidden variables from observations. Existing inference methods can be computationally expensive, require many hyperparameter choices, or support only restricted program families. This paper explores learning an inference model that can be reused across programs.

The approach treats inference as a masked prediction problem. A program supplies supervised examples containing variables and their assigned values, and some assignments are randomly hidden. A neural network learns to predict the missing values, thereby defining an approximate posterior distribution. Training a single network across multiple programs spreads the training cost across those inference problems.

The resulting foundation posterior can perform inference on new programs without additional training. It can also be specialized to a particular program and dataset through a variational inference objective. Experiments on a benchmark of STAN programs demonstrate the approach in both zero-shot and fine-tuned forms. The central idea is to make approximate inference reusable through shared predictive training.
neurips-2022-foundation-posteriors-for-a.tldr: A network trained to reconstruct masked variable assignments across probabilistic programs learns reusable approximate posteriors for zero-shot or fine-tuned inference.

paragraphs: Learned sampling methods can propose large moves through a probability distribution, but their accuracy is limited where training data are scarce, including distribution tails and high-dimensional settings. This paper studies an Explore-Exploit MCMC strategy that combines local sampling with global proposals. The aim is to benefit from both types of movement.

For this combined strategy, called Ex²MCMC, the authors prove a geometric convergence property in a weighted sense. The result does not require the global sampler to match the target distribution uniformly. They also derive explicit bounds on mixing speed under stated realistic conditions. These guarantees address a central concern with learned global proposals: imperfect coverage need not prevent the combined method from having rigorous convergence behavior.

An adaptive version, FlEx²MCMC, trains a normalizing flow during sampling and uses it to propose global moves. The authors illustrate both methods on standard sampling benchmarks and high-dimensional distributions derived from generative adversarial networks treated as energy-based models. The work combines theoretical guarantees with demonstrations of the local-global sampling design.
neurips-2022-local-global-mcmc-kernels-t.tldr: Ex²MCMC combines local and global sampling with convergence guarantees that do not require a uniformly accurate global proposal.

paragraphs: Video-language models can recognize activities with impressive generalization, yet high-level recognition tasks reveal little about their understanding of an activity's internal structure. Complex activities involve several levels of organization. This paper proposes evaluating whether models can represent the overall activity, its sub-activities, and its atomic actions together.

The authors use activity graphs as a common representation spanning all three levels and define activity parsing as generating these graphs. They introduce MOMA-LRG, a large dataset of complex human activities annotated with such structures. The annotations can also be converted into natural-language sentences, connecting structured descriptions to the language representations used by video-language models.

The paper additionally presents a lightweight, model-agnostic method for incorporating graph knowledge into video-language models during adaptation and evaluation. This is intended to address limitations of language and graphical models by combining their representations. The authors demonstrate strong few-shot activity parsing performance. The contribution broadens evaluation from recognizing an activity's name to recovering its organization across multiple levels of detail.
neurips-2022-moma-lrg-language-refined-g.tldr: MOMA-LRG evaluates detailed activity understanding through graphs linking activities, sub-activities, and atomic actions, with a dataset and lightweight video-language adaptation method.

paragraphs: A brain image contains information at several scales: small structures such as cells and blood vessels, and broader information such as the brain region it depicts. Many neuroanatomy benchmarks test only one task, leaving unclear whether a learned representation captures several kinds of structure. MTNeuro provides multiple ways to evaluate the same images.

The benchmark uses volumetric X-ray microtomography at micrometer resolution across a large thalamocortical section of mouse brain, including cortical and subcortical regions. The authors add annotations and prediction challenges covering brain-region identification and pixel-level semantic segmentation of microstructures. These tasks connect global image properties with detailed spatial information within a shared dataset.

The study evaluates several supervised and self-supervised models. Its experiments highlight the dataset's structural diversity and provide evidence about how self-supervised representations can capture multiple image attributes and support varied downstream tasks. The released data, code, and pretrained baseline models provide a common foundation for studying representation quality across levels of abstraction in brain imaging.
neurips-2022-mtneuro-a-benchmark-for-eva.tldr: MTNeuro tests whether brain-image representations capture both fine microstructures and broader regional information using multiple tasks on shared mouse-brain images.

paragraphs: Cryo-electron microscopy reconstructs molecular structures from noisy two-dimensional projections taken from unknown directions. Recovering the images' poses is therefore a key step. This paper studies pose estimation through group synchronization: combining approximate pairwise relationships into a globally consistent assignment of poses.

By examining the problem's symmetries, the authors show that relative poses in O(2), which includes planar rotations and reflections, provide sufficient constraints to identify image poses up to the molecule's chirality. That qualification leaves an ambiguity in handedness. They use this result to extend multi-frequency vector diffusion maps so that the method estimates poses as well as similarities between viewing directions.

Pose estimates can then initialize a three-dimensional reconstruction algorithm using all the input images, extending the method's role beyond clustering and averaging images. The authors validate recovery and robustness on randomly generated synchronization graphs and synthetic cryo-EM data. The contribution links a symmetry-based identification result to a more directly useful output for molecular reconstruction.
neurips-2022-on-the-symmetries-of-the-sy.tldr: Using O(2) pairwise relationships, an extended diffusion-map method recovers cryo-EM image poses up to molecular handedness and supports reconstruction initialization.

paragraphs: Estimating an average becomes difficult when observations are high-dimensional, some are corrupted, and the underlying distribution has heavy tails. This paper assumes that the true mean is sparse, meaning only a small number of its coordinates are nonzero. The goal is to exploit that structure while remaining robust to corrupted samples.

The authors give a polynomial-time estimator that is sample-efficient under mild moment assumptions. It achieves optimal asymptotic error, with sample requirements growing logarithmically in the ambient dimension. Its dependence on the desired failure probability is also optimal: requiring greater confidence adds a term proportional to the logarithm of the inverse failure probability.

The algorithm adapts a stability-based approach from robust statistics to the combined challenges of sparsity and heavy tails. Its analysis includes a specially designed non-spectral decomposition of positive semidefinite matrices with sparsity properties. The result extends efficient robust sparse mean estimation beyond previously handled light-tailed settings, while tying the guarantee to explicit distributional and sparsity assumptions.
neurips-2022-outlier-robust-sparse-mean-.tldr: Under mild moment assumptions, the paper gives an efficient outlier-robust estimator for sparse means of heavy-tailed distributions with optimal asymptotic error.

paragraphs: In multilabel classification, an example can have several correct labels, even when most possible labels do not apply. This paper studies the statistical consequences of that sparsity through upper and lower regret bounds. The measures are Hamming loss, which concerns label-wise mistakes, and Precision at κ, which concerns the selected set of κ labels.

The analysis covers two learning settings. One uses nonparametric plug-in classifiers, including approaches based on nearest neighbors. The other uses parametric models trained by minimizing empirical surrogate losses. Studying both allows the authors to examine how statistical conditions interact with different ways of constructing predictions.

The key conditions are label sparsity and a multilabel version of a low-noise assumption familiar from binary classification. The authors show that these conditions are crucial for improving the bounds, but their interaction differs between the two settings. The contribution clarifies why having few relevant labels can help statistical performance while showing that its benefit depends on the surrounding assumptions and learning approach.
neurips-2022-regret-bounds-for-multilabe.tldr: The paper shows how label sparsity and low-noise assumptions interact differently across two multilabel learning settings to improve regret bounds.

paragraphs: A randomized controlled trial may have resources to experiment on only a small fraction of a population. That creates two linked decisions: which individuals to include and how to divide them between treatment and control. This paper studies those choices jointly, aiming to estimate treatment effects accurately despite a restricted sample.

Under a linear effects model, the authors consider both individual treatment effects and the population's average effect. They develop efficient experimental designs together with corresponding estimators. Their approach draws connections to discrepancy minimization and leverage-score sampling, tools that help address balance and informative selection in mathematical computations.

The theoretical guarantees connect smoothly to established results when the experimental sample expands to include the whole population. This makes the constrained setting part of a broader design problem with a familiar full-population endpoint. The authors also demonstrate their algorithms empirically. The main contribution is treating representative selection and treatment-control assignment as a coordinated task under the stated linear modeling assumption.
neurips-2022-sample-constrained-treatmen.tldr: Under a linear effects model, the paper jointly designs participant selection and treatment-control assignment for trials with severely limited sample sizes.

paragraphs: Inverse problems infer quantities such as physical parameters or control inputs from desired or observed outcomes. Machine learning can accelerate repeated inference, but training through a physical process can be difficult. The authors identify strongly varying gradients from nonlinear physics as a reason first-order optimizers such as SGD and Adam may choose suboptimal directions.

Their method combines machine learning with higher-order optimization. A scale-invariant inverse problem solver supplies updates that are inserted into a gradient-descent learning pipeline, replacing the ordinary gradient of the physical process. This allows the training procedure to use directions produced by a solver designed for the inverse problem while retaining a gradient-based learning framework.

The authors demonstrate the approach on a variety of canonical physical systems and report significant improvements across optimization and learning problems. The contribution is a specific connection between physical inversion and network training: updates from the inverse solver become part of how the model learns. The reported findings support this hybrid approach for the physical problems examined.
neurips-2022-scale-invariant-learning-by.tldr: The method improves learning for tested physical inverse problems by replacing ordinary physics gradients with updates from a scale-invariant inverse solver.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a compact image representation can retain meaningful information about the shapes that generated an image. It studies a mathematical setting in which synthetic images are formed from unions or intersections of specified shapes. Thresholded polynomial functions describe those shapes, with ellipses and rectangles given as examples.

The authors construct a succinct sketch whose relationship to the underlying shape coefficients is smooth. That connection gives the representation an explicit relationship to latent image attributes. They prove that images can be reconstructed easily from their sketches and that similar shapes produce similar sketches, linking compactness to recoverable and similarity-preserving information.

The sketches also support indexing to retrieve similar images or image parts. A dictionary can store shared concepts and shape attributes, allowing matching parts within or across images to reference the same entry. These guarantees apply to the specified synthetic-image model. The contribution is a provable connection between a compact representation, its generating shapes, and operations such as reconstruction, retrieval, and attribute sharing.
neurips-2022-sketching-based-representat.tldr: For synthetic images built from specified shapes, the paper constructs compact sketches with guarantees for reconstruction, similarity preservation, retrieval, and shared shape representations.

paragraphs: Dale's principle divides biological neurons into excitatory and inhibitory types. This restricts the possible architectures of a network, raising a question about what those restrictions mean for computation and learning. The paper investigates that question using recurrent spiking networks and rate-based network models.

The authors find that Daleian networks can closely approximate computations performed by networks without this restriction, despite having an exponentially smaller set of possible architectures. They also find greater functional robustness to noise in synaptic connections. Together, these results suggest that the structural constraint can coexist with strong computational capability and may confer a robustness benefit in the models studied.

The learning results concern what needs to be adjusted. Daleian networks can learn efficiently by tuning features of individual neurons, nearly matching learning that adjusts individual synaptic weights. The authors report that this does not hold similarly for non-Daleian networks. They interpret the finding as support for simpler, more biologically plausible learning mechanisms and as a direction for designing artificial networks.
neurips-2022-the-computational-and-learn.tldr: The studied Daleian networks closely reproduce unrestricted computations, show greater resistance to synaptic noise, and learn effectively through neuron-level adjustments.

paragraphs: Coordinating two dexterous hands is difficult for reinforcement learning because many joints must work together. Bi-DexHands provides a simulator and benchmark with tens of two-handed manipulation tasks and thousands of target objects. The tasks are designed using cognitive-science descriptions of human motor skills and implemented in Isaac Gym for efficient training.

The benchmark examines several learning settings, including multi-agent, offline, multi-task, and meta reinforcement learning. The authors report that PPO-type on-policy methods learn simple tasks associated with motor skills up to those of a 48-month-old child, such as catching an object or opening a bottle. Multi-agent methods further help with tasks requiring coordinated use of both hands.

Success on separate tasks does not translate reliably into mastering multiple skills. Existing algorithms fail on most of the benchmark's multi-task and few-shot learning tasks. This separates progress in learning individual simulated manipulations from the broader challenge of acquiring reusable skills. The benchmark supplies a structured way to study both capabilities and the remaining gap between them.
neurips-2022-towards-human-level-bimanua.tldr: Bi-DexHands benchmarks two-handed robotic manipulation, revealing success on individual tasks but substantial difficulty with multi-task and few-shot skill learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies transition to linearity in very wide feedforward neural networks. Its focus is architectural generality: the networks can follow arbitrary directed acyclic graphs, so the result is not tied to a single standard arrangement of layers. The authors show that this broader class undergoes the transition as width tends to infinity.

A key part of the contribution is defining width for these general graphs. The definition uses the smallest number of incoming connections among neurons, excluding the input and first layers. This expresses width through connectivity and provides a common quantity for architectures whose graph structures can differ. The limiting statement concerns this measure growing without bound.

The authors identify mathematical structure underlying the transition and extend earlier results about linearity or constancy of the Neural Tangent Kernel in standard architectures. The significance is a unified architectural scope for a phenomenon previously characterized in more specific network families. The result concerns an infinite-width limit, which is the setting of the paper's stated claim.
neurips-2022-transition-to-linearity-of-.tldr: Feedforward networks on arbitrary directed acyclic graphs exhibit transition to linearity as a connectivity-based measure of width tends to infinity.

paragraphs: Post hoc explanation methods often appear to pursue different goals, making it difficult to understand their relationships or choose between them. This paper places eight popular methods in a common framework, including LIME, KernelSHAP, Occlusion, gradient-based explanations, SmoothGrad, and Integrated Gradients. The shared task is approximating a black-box model locally.

Within this framework, the methods differ in the neighborhood where they approximate the model and the loss function used to judge that approximation. Those choices make the intended meaning of faithfulness more explicit: an explanation is evaluated against particular model behavior around an input. The framework therefore connects method selection to the behavior one wants the explanation to reproduce.

The authors prove a no-free-lunch result showing that no explanation method is optimal across all neighborhoods. They also derive a principle for choosing methods based on faithfulness and validate their theoretical results across datasets, model classes, and prediction tasks. The contribution gives both a conceptual account of existing methods and a principled basis for selecting among them.
neurips-2022-which-explanation-should-i-.tldr: Eight explanation methods share a local approximation objective, and choosing among them depends on the neighborhood and faithfulness criterion that matter.
